title: Mecca Defense Pact Binds Turkey to Saudi-Pakistan Mutual Defense, Baykar Production Locks Into Saudi, Hormuz Deal Nears
subhead: Saudi Arabia, Turkey, and Pakistan sign a NATO-style mutual defense agreement in Mecca — 'attack on one is attack on all' — creating a formal framework for Turkish drone production in Saudi Arabia, as the US signals an Iran-Oman deal to reopen Hormuz could come within days and Israel's foreign minister accuses Ankara of hypocrisy over its Syria and Cyprus presence.

sections.heading: Mecca Joint Defense Agreement Signed by Saudi Arabia, Turkey, and Pakistan
sections.body:
Saudi Arabia, Turkey, and Pakistan signed the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement on Aug. 7, the first formal military pact among the three leading Sunni powers. Under its terms, an attack on any of the three states will be regarded as an attack on all, the Pakistani Foreign Ministry said in a statement. The agreement was signed in Mecca by Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, and Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, according to Reuters, Al-Monitor, and the AP.

The timing and venue — a Friday, the Muslim holy day, in Mecca — underscore the pact's religious symbolism. Saudi deputy minister for public diplomacy Rayed Krimly stressed the agreement did not 'represent an effort to establish a military axis or a sectarian bloc,' Al-Monitor reported. But diplomats briefing Al-Monitor on background said there is little doubt the pact is aimed at countering Shiite Iran's influence.

The pact builds on a bilateral Pakistan-Saudi defense agreement signed in September 2025 and follows Pakistan's April deployment of a fighter jet squadron and Chinese-made air defense systems to a Saudi airbase. An immediate question is whether Turkey will follow suit and deploy forces — including naval assets — to Saudi Arabia, expanding a military footprint that already includes its largest overseas base in Somalia and an undisclosed number of troops in Qatar, Al-Monitor reported.

Israel is likely to perceive the agreement as a threat, according to Gallia Lindenstrauss, a senior researcher at the Institute for National Security Studies in Israel. 'It adds a military component to a political front that has presented a firm anti-Israel stance,' she told Al-Monitor, noting that it also makes Saudi-Israeli normalization less likely. Egypt, under President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi, notably did not join the pact despite being part of the emerging 'Quad' with Riyadh, Ankara, and Islamabad — a signal that the agreement's religious overtones and Turkey's involvement are causes for caution, a regional diplomat told Al-Monitor: 'Anyone with half a brain would have kept Mecca out of it.'
sections.whyItMatters: The Mecca pact is the first formal military alliance binding Turkey to Saudi Arabia and Pakistan — a trio that brings together NATO's second-largest army, the Muslim world's only nuclear power, and the Gulf's most important military spender. The question diplomats raise is whether the mutual defense clause would actually be invoked: 'That is a claim to be tested,' one told Al-Monitor. Without US buy-in and with Israel explicitly threatened, the pact's deterrence value is uncertain, but its political signaling is unmistakable.

sections.heading: Baykar Drone Production Locked Into Saudi Arabia Under Pact Framework
sections.body:
The Mecca defense pact creates a formal framework for Turkey's Baykar to deepen drone co-production inside Saudi Arabia, accelerating Riyadh's push to manufacture rather than merely buy its weapons and reduce decades of dependency on US arms suppliers, MSN reported.

The agreement dovetails with the record trajectory of Turkey's defense exports, which reached $5.79 billion in the first seven months of 2026 — a 26.2% year-on-year increase — with the trailing 12-month total hitting $11.2 billion, Defense Industry Agency head Haluk Gorgun announced, according to Al-Monitor. Rockets, missiles, and smart munitions have emerged as Turkey's largest defense export category at $3.7 billion in sales last year, while UAV exports reached $2.1 billion.

Baykar, Turkey's largest drone manufacturer, has been expanding aggressively: it signed its first Kizilelma export agreement with Indonesia in May covering 12 aircraft with options for 48 more, and a deal with the UAE's EDGE Group in May 2026 to integrate EDGE-made guided weapons onto Baykar drones. ASELSAN, Turkey's largest defense electronics firm, signed $629 million in new export contracts during the first quarter, up 69% year-on-year.
sections.whyItMatters: The pact formalizes a defense-industrial dimension that goes beyond symbolism. Turkey is moving from selling drones to Saudi Arabia to building them there — a model that embeds Turkish defense technology in Gulf infrastructure and creates long-term maintenance, training, and upgrade dependencies. For the US, the narrowing gap in Turkish-Saudi defense cooperation reduces the leverage that American arms sales have traditionally provided.

sections.heading: US Signals Hormuz Deal Imminent as Oil Prices Swing on Conflicting Signals
sections.body:
A US official reported progress between Iran and Oman that could soon reopen the Strait of Hormuz, potentially restoring oil exports disrupted by the five-month-old US-Iran war, Reuters reported on Aug. 7. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said a ceasefire and Hormuz deal could come within days.

Oil prices swung violently on conflicting signals. Crude jumped nearly 4% on Thursday after Iran's parliament began reviewing a bill that would impose shipping curbs in the Strait of Hormuz, including a ban on US- and Israeli-linked vessels and transit tolls, Pakistan Today and CNA reported. The same day, prices were pulled in the opposite direction by hopes for an Iran-Oman deal — oil had already tumbled 7% on Aug. 3 after Trump canceled a massive strike on Iran and signaled negotiations would resume, Reuters reported.

For Turkey, Hormuz is a double-edged vulnerability: the strait handles roughly 15-20% of Turkey's crude imports, and any closure or toll regime directly raises energy costs for an economy still battling inflation. A rapid reopening would ease that pressure; a formal Iranian toll regime would not.
sections.whyItMatters: The competing signals — Iran's parliament reviewing Hormuz curbs while US officials tout an imminent deal — capture the volatility of the moment. For Turkey, a Hormuz reopening would be an immediate economic relief, but the structural risk remains: any formalized Iranian toll or inspection regime sets a precedent for chokepoint extortion that Ankara cannot control.

sections.heading: Israel Accuses Turkey of Hypocrisy Over Syria and Cyprus
sections.body:
Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar accused Turkey of hypocrisy on Friday, saying Ankara continues to occupy territory in both Syria and Cyprus while criticizing Israel's military actions, the Cleveland Jewish News and Israel National News reported.

Saar said Turkey 'occupies parts of Syria' while criticizing Israel for maintaining a narrow security buffer against terrorist threats. He also pointed to Turkey's military presence in Northern Cyprus, which has been sustained since 1974. The exchange came as Israeli strikes in southern Syria continued, and after Foreign Minister Fidan's Aug. 6 press conference with Syrian Foreign Minister Shibani where he called Israeli attacks 'among the greatest threats to the country's stability.'

Israel's response is significant because Turkey is the only one of the three Mecca pact signatories that formally recognizes Israel. The growing rift between Ankara and Jerusalem has accelerated since the Gaza war, and the defense pact — which Israel perceives as threatening — further narrows the already diminishing space for diplomatic repair.
sections.whyItMatters: Saar's accusation crystallizes the tension in Turkey's regional posture: Ankara positions itself as a defender of sovereignty and critic of occupation while maintaining troops in Syria and Northern Cyprus. The Mecca pact amplifies this contradiction — Israel sees a military alliance that includes a country occupying Syrian territory lecturing Israel about its own buffer zone. The diplomatic damage is cumulative and probably irreversible in the near term.

sections.heading: Turkey Joins Saudi-Led Red Sea Maritime Coalition
sections.body:
Turkey and Pakistan are among 14 countries that signed the joint communique establishing Saudi Arabia's Multinational Maritime Defense Coalition for the Red Sea, Bab al-Mandeb, and Gulf of Aden, Al-Monitor reported. The coalition, announced July 30, aims to protect international shipping and energy supply routes from Houthi attacks.

The signing comes as Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia intensify: a Saudi official said the kingdom expects imminent two-pronged attacks from the north (Iran) and south (Houthis), Reuters reported. Houthis killed 30+ soldiers in Yemen's oil-rich Marib province with 12+ missile and drone attacks on Friday, CBS News reported. The UAE, Bahrain, and Kuwait condemned the Houthi strikes.

Al-Monitor's sources noted that Turkey's participation was surprising given its reluctance to take a subordinate role under Saudi command in military operations. The coalition will meet again Aug. 12-13 to finalize its institutional framework. The US has not yet formally committed, despite being invited.
sections.whyItMatters: Turkey's decision to join the Red Sea coalition — and sign the Mecca pact the same week — signals a deliberate expansion of its military-diplomatic footprint in the Gulf. But Ankara is committing to two overlapping security frameworks in which it will not be in charge, which is uncharacteristic. The real test comes when Turkish naval assets are asked to engage Houthi targets directly.

sections.heading: Mohamed Salah Signs Two-Year Trabzonspor Contract
sections.body:
Former Liverpool star Mohamed Salah signed a two-year contract with Trabzonspor on Aug. 7, the club announced, according to USA Today, Reuters, and the NYT Athletic. The 34-year-old Egypt captain arrived at Istanbul airport on Wednesday wearing Trabzonspor's burgundy and blue kit, where hundreds of fans greeted him.

Salah called the experience 'something I never had in my life' at his opening press conference. 'I'm here to win. I want to win something with this club because you guys showed me so much love,' he said. The deal follows nine seasons at Liverpool where he scored 257 goals and won the Champions League and two Premier League titles.

Trabzonspor finished third in the 2025-26 Super Lig and is entering the UEFA Europa League playoff round. The club also signed Cape Verde international Sidny Lopes Cabral, whose World Cup goal against Argentina was named the tournament's best, under manager Fatih Tekke.
sections.whyItMatters: Beyond sport, Salah's arrival is a branding windfall for Trabzon and Turkish football. Salah's global profile brings attention and tourism potential to a city that has long leveraged its club as an economic engine. For Trabzonspor — a club with a passionate fanbase but limited Champions League resources — the signing signals ambition and deep-pocketed backing, even if the competitive upside of a 34-year-old in a physical league is a fair question.

sections.heading: Anti-Terror Bill Commission Review Begins as Government Targets Aug. 11 Passage
sections.body:
Parliament's Justice Commission began reviewing the government-backed 'Law on Strengthening National Solidarity and Social Integration' on Aug. 7, Anadolu Agency reported, with the ruling bloc aiming to complete passage by Aug. 11 before the legislature goes into recess.

The bill, submitted with approximately 360 lawmaker signatures on Aug. 5, creates the legal framework for suspending PKK/KCK investigations and sentences after the National Security Council certifies the group has disbanded. The six-month application window after the MGK decision, the 5-to-10-year suspension periods, and the coordination board chaired by Vice President Cevdet Yilmaz all remain as previously outlined. A 17-member parliamentary monitoring commission would also be created.

Al-Monitor reported that Turkey is seeking Baghdad's assistance for the demobilization and disarmament of PKK fighters who qualify, with Iraqi Supreme Judicial Council president Faiq Zeidan meeting Erdogan on Thursday. The PKK's armed fighters are based primarily in Kurdish-controlled northern Iraq.
sections.whyItMatters: The commission review is proceeding on schedule. The government's Aug. 11 target is aggressive but achievable given the supermajority backing. The more consequential unknowns — whether Öcalan is mentioned, how the Kurdish political movement responds, and whether Baghdad cooperates on demobilization — are outside the commission room.

bottomLine: The Mecca Joint Defense Agreement is the day's defining development: it binds Turkey to a mutual defense commitment with Saudi Arabia and Pakistan for the first time, locks Baykar drone production into Saudi infrastructure, and draws an immediate Israeli accusation of hypocrisy. The overlapping Red Sea coalition commitment means Turkey has signed onto two Gulf security frameworks in a single week — a rapid expansion of its military-diplomatic footprint that comes with real escalation risk if Houthi or Iranian attacks trigger the mutual defense clause. The anti-terror bill's commission review is on track for Aug. 11 passage, the US signals a Hormuz deal could come within days, and Salah's Trabzonspor signing is a cultural and economic milestone for a city that treats its club as an institution.
sources: Reuters, Al-Monitor, Anadolu Agency, AP, USA Today, NYT Athletic, MSN, Pakistan Today, Channel News Asia, CBS News, Israel National News, Cleveland Jewish News, MoneyControl, India TV News, Irish Times
